channel.title: The MisterLibrarian Bible Project
channel.description: A fresh translation of the Bible into modern English, made from the original Hebrew and Greek one chapter at a time.

item.title: Joshua 17
item.description: Manasseh's own lot falls with the rare verb Joshua 16 promised — 'the lot WAS,' matching Judah's own rank rather than Ephraim's — and Zelophehad's five daughters draw near a second time, forty years after Numbers 27, to collect an inheritance they now quote back in the law's…

item.title: Joshua 16
item.description: The second lot goes out — and the verb is the find: 'the lot WENT OUT,' not the 'lot WAS' that opened Judah's own chapter and opens Manasseh's next door, the one grammatical mark on these pages that tells the brother who outranks every other tribe from the brother who, after…

item.title: Joshua 15
item.description: The lot finally falls — the exact sentence Joshua 14 promised — and Judah's border runs clean past Jerusalem without claiming it, fifty-five verses before the chapter's own last line admits the Jebusites were never driven out. Caleb's own grant from chapter 14 is carried out…

item.title: Joshua 14
item.description: Eleazar the priest is named before Joshua, and steps into the book for the first time — every battle so far was fought without him. Then Caleb, eighty-five years old, walks up to Joshua at Gilgal and asks for the one thing no lot will ever decide: Hebron, and the Anakim still…

item.title: Joshua 13
item.description: The war is over and Jehovah's first word is that it isn't: 'very much land' still remains — Philistia, the Lebanon coast — and the command to allot it anyway uses the Bible's own verb for casting a lot, before a single lot is cast. Moses' old grant to Reuben, Gad and half of…

item.title: Joshua 12
item.description: The war over, the roll call begins: two kings Moses struck east of the Jordan — Sihon of Heshbon, Og of Bashan, 'one of the remnant of the Rephaim' — recapped in six verses before Joshua's own thirty-one, named two to a verse in a bare counting formula with no story left in…

item.title: Luke 24
item.description: The tomb is open and empty, and the first witnesses to the resurrection are told, in a question no other Gospel asks, why they are seeking the living among the dead — a report the Eleven call nonsense, in a Greek word that occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Two…

item.title: Luke 23
item.description: Jesus is led before Pilate on a three-part political charge found in no other Gospel, then shuttled to Herod for a hearing found nowhere else either — Herod gets to see him perform nothing but silence, and strikes up an unlikely friendship with Pilate the same day. Pilate…

item.title: Luke 22
item.description: Satan enters Judas by name, and the plot against Jesus finds its instrument from inside the Twelve. A Passover meal becomes a supper the Christian world has never stopped repeating — bread and a cup named "my body" and "the new covenant in my blood," on a reading of the text…

item.title: Luke 21
item.description: A poor widow drops two small coins into the temple treasury and is declared, by Jesus' own verdict, to have given more than every rich giver beside her. Admirers of the temple's stonework are told not one stone will be left on another — and Luke's own version of the question…

item.title: Luke 20
item.description: The chief priests and scribes demand to know by what authority Jesus is acting, and are trapped by a counter-question about John the Baptist that leaves them unable to answer either way. Jesus then tells the crowd — not the leaders themselves — a parable found in all three…

item.title: Luke 19
item.description: A short, rich chief tax collector named Zacchaeus climbs a sycamore-fig tree to see Jesus over a crowd at Jericho, and is called down by name and told salvation has come to his house — "he too is a son of Abraham," the identical phrase this Gospel has already spoken of only…

item.title: Luke 18
item.description: A widow wears down an unjust judge by sheer persistence, and Jesus argues from a corrupt court to a God who is neither corrupt nor slow. A Pharisee and a tax collector pray two very different prayers in the same temple, and the one who asks God for mercy — not the one who…

item.title: Luke 17
item.description: A warning about stumbling blocks and a call to forgive a repeat offender seven times in one day gives way to the apostles asking for more faith, and Jesus answering with the identical "faith like a grain of mustard seed" this project has already translated once in Matthew …

item.title: Luke 16
item.description: A manager caught wasting his master’s property — the identical verb the prodigal son squandered his own inheritance with, one chapter earlier — writes down his master’s debtors’ bills before he is fired, buying himself a soft landing on someone else’s money; the master ends…

item.title: Luke 15
item.description: Tax collectors and sinners keep drawing near to hear Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes mutter the identical charge this Gospel has already recorded once — so Jesus answers with three parables instead of one more defense. A shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep in the…

item.title: Luke 14
item.description: A man with dropsy is healed on the Sabbath at a Pharisee ruler’s own table, and the Sabbath argument this Gospel already lost two chapters ago returns sharper — a SON now named beside the ox that falls in a well. Watching the guests scramble for the best couches, Jesus tells…

item.title: Luke 13
item.description: Word of Galileans whose blood Pilate mixed with their own sacrifices, and of eighteen killed when a tower falls at Siloam, gets the identical answer twice over: neither proves the dead were the worse sinners, only that everyone else needs to turn around. A fig tree that…

item.title: Luke 12
item.description: A crowd gathered “by the tens of thousands,” trampling each other, hears Jesus turn first to twelve of them — fear God rather than an executioner who “has nothing more” to do, sparrows sold five for two pennies (a better rate than Matthew’s), and the one sin this Gospel will…

item.title: Luke 11
item.description: A disciple asks to be taught to pray, and gets Luke’s own shorter Lord’s Prayer — no “our,” no “in heaven,” no third petition — followed by a friend roused from bed at midnight by nothing but his own shamelessness (or is it the asker’s?), and “ask, seek, knock” ending on a…

item.title: Luke 10
item.description: Seventy-two are sent out ahead of him in pairs — “lambs in the midst of wolves” — and return rejoicing that even the demons submit, only to be told to rejoice instead that their names are written in heaven; Jesus watches “Satan fall from heaven like lightning” and, in the…

item.title: Joshua 11
item.description: The war turns north. Jabin king of Hazor raises a coalition as numerous as the sand on the seashore — the exact words once used of Abraham's own promised descendants — and Israel falls on it by surprise at the waters of Merom. Joshua hamstrings the enemy's horses on command…

item.title: Luke 9
item.description: The Twelve are sent out with nothing for the road and given, of all things, Jesus’s own “power and authority”; a crowd of thousands is fed from five loaves and two fish; and Herod, having beheaded John, asks a question this Gospel keeps widening — “who is this?” — until Peter…

item.title: Luke 8
item.description: Women who fund the ministry out of their own means, among them Mary Magdalene, introduced by name for the first time; a sower whose seed falls on four soils, interpreted verse by verse for the disciples alone once the crowd is gone; a storm silenced by a rebuke, the disciples…

item.title: Luke 7
item.description: A centurion who never meets Jesus sends word that he is “not worthy” to have him under his roof — and Jesus marvels, the only time in Luke that he does. At the gate of Nain a widow’s only son is given back to her in the very words of Elijah, and for the first time the…

item.title: Luke 6
item.description: Grain plucked on the sabbath, a withered hand healed in a synagogue watching for a charge, and a whole night in prayer before the Twelve are named — including the payoff of a name planted a chapter early, “Simon, whom he also named Peter.” Coming down to “a level place,” not…

item.title: Luke 5
item.description: By the lake of Gennesaret the Simon whose house was already named a chapter early is called at last, after a catch of fish that breaks the nets; a leper is touched and cleansed, a paralyzed man is let down through a roof, and the crowd says, “We have seen incredible things…

item.title: Joshua 10
item.description: Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem — the first time the Bible names the city — raises five Amorite kings against Gibeon for making peace with Israel. Joshua marches all night from Gilgal, hailstones kill more than the sword on the Beth-horon road, and Joshua speaks to the sun…

item.title: Luke 4
item.description: Full of the Spirit and led in the wilderness, Jesus is tested three times in words from Deuteronomy, and in Luke the devil explains that the kingdoms of the inhabited world “have been handed over to me”. At Nazareth he reads Isaiah 61 and rolls up the scroll mid-verse, before…

item.title: Luke 3
item.description: Luke dates John’s first sermon by seven rulers — the fifteenth year of Tiberius, Pilate, three tetrarchs and a high priest with two names — then quotes Isaiah on to “all flesh shall see the salvation of God”, a line the Hebrew does not have. Only Luke has crowds, tax…
